# Education in Nigeria
Education in Nigeria consists of a structured system beginning with primary education at around age five, lasting six years, followed by secondary education divided into three years of junior secondary school and three years of senior secondary school under the Universal Basic Education (UBE) framework. Primary education includes core subjects such as Mathematics, English, Religious Knowledge, Agricultural Science, Home Economics, and one of the main indigenous languages (Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba, or Igbo), with private schools offering additional courses like Computer Science and French. Secondary education builds on this with compulsory core subjects complemented by electives, and technical colleges offer vocational training leading to trade certificates. Federal and state governments manage public secondary schools, with federal colleges known as "unity schools" regarded as elite, while state schools often struggle with funding, staffing shortages, and infrastructure challenges. Private secondary schools generally have smaller classes, modern facilities, and better-qualified teachers but are considerably more expensive.
Promotional examinations necessitate completing mandatory schooling phases aligning with the 9-3-4 system, with students taking the Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE) or General Certificate of Education (GCE), administered by the West African Examination Council (WAEC) and the National Examination Council (NECO). Nigeria also offers advanced level programs like the Interim Joint Matriculation Board (IJMB) and Joint Universities Preliminary Examinations Board (JUPEB) for direct university entry. Higher education includes federal, state, and private universities with various durations depending on courses, alongside polytechnics and colleges of education. Vocational education remains primarily informal, challenged by inadequate resources and quality concerns. Literacy rates remain a significant challenge, with ongoing governmental and NGO efforts targeting improvements, including female education initiatives and combating regional disparities.
